title: Hegemony and Ideology

cards.h: Why do people obey without being forced?
cards.b:
A ruler cannot guard every citizen with a soldier. Most rule works because people accept it, or even like it. How does this acceptance get made? Two key concepts answer: ideology and hegemony.

Ideology is a system of ideas that makes sense of the world and guides action. Hegemony is leadership by consent: a ruling group wins the approval of others, so its interests look like everyone's.

Together they extend the study of power from visible force to culture, schools, media, religion and common sense. This is the third face of power (Lukes), brought out in the last lesson.

Both appear regularly in the exam, especially Gramsci, Althusser and the Frankfurt School. A good answer compares the Marxist view with non-Marxist ones.

The word was coined by the French thinker Destutt de Tracy (1796) as a "science of ideas". Napoleon mocked such thinkers as "ideologues". Since then it has gone through several meanings.

  • Neutral: any belief system about how society should be (liberalism, socialism).
  • Critical (Marx): ideas that distort reality and hide class domination. False consciousness is the later term (Engels, 1893).
  • Sociological (Mannheim): all thought is shaped by social position (Ideology and Utopia, 1929). He distinguished ideology (ideas defending the order) from utopia (ideas challenging it).

Heywood says an ideology has three elements: a view of the existing order, a model of the desired future and a way to get there.

cards.h: Marx: ideology and the ruling class
cards.b:
In The German Ideology (written 1845-46, published 1932), Marx and Engels wrote that the ideas of the ruling class are, in every age, the ruling ideas. The class that controls material production also controls the production of ideas.

Ideology therefore serves to:

  • Present class interests as universal ("the national interest").
  • Make existing arrangements seem natural and eternal (e.g., private property, the market).
  • Hide exploitation: a wage looks like a fair exchange.

Marx also wrote of commodity fetishism (Capital, 1867): social relations appear as relations between things. Religion, he wrote, is the "opium of the people" (1844).

Later Lukacs, History and Class Consciousness (1923), developed reification and said the proletariat could reach true class consciousness.

Antonio Gramsci wrote the Prison Notebooks (1929-35) in Mussolini's jail. He asked why revolution had succeeded in Russia but failed in the West. His answer: in the West, the ruling class holds power through hegemony, cultural and moral leadership in civil society, not just force.

  • The state is "hegemony protected by the armour of coercion".
  • Ideas become common sense, accepted without question.
  • The working class must build a counter-hegemony through a long war of position (a struggle for culture and institutions), not only a quick war of manoeuvre (direct assault).
  • Organic intellectuals arise from each class and give it self-awareness.
  • A historic bloc joins economic base and ideology.

See lesson 0-9-7 for more.

Louis Althusser, "Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses" (1970)

Distinguished Repressive State Apparatuses (army, police, courts) from Ideological State Apparatuses (schools, churches, media, family). The school is the chief ISA of modern capitalism. Ideology "interpellates" individuals: it hails them and makes them see themselves as subjects with certain roles. Ideology has a material existence in practices.

Frankfurt School

Horkheimer and Adorno, Dialectic of Enlightenment (1944): the culture industry (films, radio) makes people passive consumers. Herbert Marcuse, One-Dimensional Man (1964): advanced capitalism flattens critical thought through consumerism. His separate essay "Repressive Tolerance" (1965) argued that tolerance in such a society can shield domination.

Both go beyond Marx in treating culture as a major site of domination.

If ideas can make people accept their lot, is resistance possible? Several writers say yes.

  • James C. Scott, Weapons of the Weak (1985), studied Malaysian peasants. They resist through foot-dragging, gossip, petty theft and sabotage, not open revolt. Scott's Domination and the Arts of Resistance (1990) describes a public transcript (the polite face shown to the powerful) and a hidden transcript (what the subordinate say among themselves). Thus apparent consent can hide disbelief.
  • Gramsci: common sense is contradictory. People hold both ruling ideas and ideas from their own experience. This opens a gap for a counter-hegemony.
  • Foucault: where there is power, there is resistance.
  • Feminist and Dalit movements challenge common sense by renaming experience, e.g., "sexual harassment", "manual scavenging" or "atrocity".

Hegemony is never complete. It must be renewed constantly, and it can be lost.

cards.h: End of ideology? End of history?
cards.b:
• Daniel Bell, The End of Ideology (1960): in the post-war West, the big ideological battles had faded, replaced by technical, welfare-state consensus.
  • Francis Fukuyama, "The End of History?" (1989) and The End of History and the Last Man (1992): after the Cold War, liberal democracy has no serious rival.
  • Reply: new ideologies returned. Samuel Huntington's Clash of Civilizations (1996), religious fundamentalism, populism, nationalism and environmentalism show that ideology did not end.
  • Post-Marxists: Laclau and Mouffe, Hegemony and Socialist Strategy (1985), see hegemony as a contest of discourses among many groups, not only classes.

Note too that claiming "no ideology" is itself an ideological move, as Marxists say.

The term is also used in Paper II.

  • Hegemonic stability theory (Charles Kindleberger, The World in Depression, 1973; Robert Gilpin, War and Change in World Politics, 1981): an open world economy needs one leading power to provide public goods.
  • Neo-Gramscian IR (Robert Cox, 1981, "Social Forces, States and World Orders"): hegemony is a world order built on consent as well as power, with international institutions (IMF, World Bank, WTO) spreading dominant ideas.
  • Mearsheimer defines hegemon in offensive realism as the sole great power.
  • Edward Said, Orientalism (1978): Western knowledge of the East served imperial domination, a cultural hegemony using Foucault's power/knowledge.

• Caste: Phule, Gulamgiri (1873), and Ambedkar, Annihilation of Caste (1936), saw caste as an ideology of Brahmanical dominance, made to seem sacred and natural. Ambedkar's "graded inequality" explains why the oppressed rarely unite.
  • Colonial: Macaulay's Minute (1835) aimed to create a class of Indians loyal in taste and opinion. Ranajit Guha, Dominance without Hegemony (1997), argued the British Raj ruled by dominance (coercion) because it never won Indian consent. Subaltern Studies (from 1982) drew on Gramsci to study peasant politics.
  • Nationalism: Congress under Gandhi built a broad hegemonic bloc (a "passive revolution", said Partha Chatterjee after Gramsci).
  • Today: debates on cultural nationalism, media power and social media narratives are often framed as contests of hegemony and counter-hegemony. Gramsci is a favourite lens in these essays, but present evidence from both sides.

"Hegemony is the key concept in Gramsci's political thought." Discuss.
Compare the Marxist and non-Marxist views of ideology.
Examine the role of Ideological State Apparatuses in maintaining capitalism.
Is the 'end of ideology' thesis valid?

Structure: define ideology and give its three senses. Give the Marxist line (German Ideology, false consciousness) and then Gramsci's hegemony with its main terms. Add Althusser, the Frankfurt School and Mannheim. Take the 'end of ideology' debate (Bell, Fukuyama) as the critique. Close with Indian examples such as caste ideology and Guha's dominance without hegemony.
